text: Hi, everyone. I'm Joseph Kim, and I lead ChatGBT for Financial Services, a new product we launched just one month ago. Many of you have already experienced how tools like Codex have changed the way you build in software engineering. AI has become a much bigger part of the work you do every day. Mobile intelligence is continuing to improve at an incredible pace, but many people working industries like finance haven't yet experienced that same change in their day-to-day work. I expect that to start changing rapidly over the next few months, and builders like all of you in this room have a big role in making that happen quickly, taking the intelligence in these models and turning it into products that people can use in their daily work. Today, I will share a little bit about what we learned building ChatGBT for Financial Services and how we're thinking about what comes next. I'll start by showing you what we've built, including a quick demo. Then I'll explain why we built it and why we think now is the right time to build. From there, I'll walk you through how we built it with some technical lessons that I hope you can apply to your own products. Finally, we'll take a look at where models are headed and products are going and what that can mean for financial work over the next year. Let's start with what we've built. ChatGBT for Financial Services is a tailored version of ChatGBT work built specifically for financial professionals, starting with investment banking and equity research. It's designed to help people at the large financial institutions get more out of their day-to-day work, similar to how Codex speeds you up in software development. As we built the product with our design partners, Morgan Stanley and Evercore, we focused on three core areas. First, financial data. Financial data is the foundation of financial work, and the work you can do is limited by the quality of your sources. We wanted people to have access to the data they need directly within ChatGBT. Second, an interface built for finance. We wanted the product to feel familiar to financial professionals with ways to inspect source material, explore financial charts, and control the sources behind an analysis. Third, your firm's format. Financial work happens within the context of an organization, and the models and presentations people produce need to follow their firm's format and standards. We made it easier to create those artifacts using firm-specific templates. But they say a picture's worth a thousand words, so I'll stop talking for a bit and show you the product. Wonderful, now I'd like to take some time to talk about why we built it. We built ChatGBT for financial services to help close what we call the capability overhang. As you can see here, model capabilities have improved at a tremendous rate over the last few years. In just a few years, we've gone from models solving high school math problems to systems capable of solving millennial-prized math problems. But the value people get from these models in their day-to-day work hasn't kept pace. You read about the breakthroughs in the news, yet for many financial professionals, the way they work hasn't changed nearly as quickly. We call that gap the capability overhang, the distance between what the model is capable of and the value people can actually get from it. Closing that gap takes more than building a capable model. People need the right data and tools, and they need an experience that fits the way they work. That's where builders like you come in. I want to show you an example of how much of a difference the right product experience can make. This is a chart that shows how codecs usage grew within OpenAI across different job functions. As you can see, engineers started using codecs early, and that share grew steadily. But look at finance, legal, and recruiting. At the beginning of 2026, almost none of their AI output was generated in codecs. By June, that share was around 90%. If you look carefully, you'll notice a huge inflection point that happened around February-March of this year. I went back to see what happened around this time, assuming that we must have released a new model, but instead I found that we had released the codecs desktop app in February. My takeaway is that the product made it easier for people outside of engineering to put these capabilities to work. That's the opportunity we're pursuing in finance, building an experience that helps financial professionals get much more value from the intelligence already available to them. Now let me talk about how we built it. Let's start with data. In finance, the work you can do is limited by the quality of the information you have access to. So we wanted the product to come with the sources professionals rely on, from financial statements and earning transcripts to market and private company data. We looked at existing MCP connectors for financial data and found that many had issues with latency, errors, or search quality. So we went and licensed a lot of this data directly and built our own hosting and search indices using the same infrastructure as our web index. We still use the MCP protocol to give the model access to the data, but hosting and indexing it ourselves gives us more control over the quality and the reliability of the experience. It also gives us the flexibility to post-train our models to work with these datasets. The analogy I like to use is MCP and skills are like handing an instruction manual to a junior analyst versus post-training, where the model is like having a senior analyst who's been working with the data for over two decades and knows all of its quirks like the back of their hand. MCP and skills give the model access and instructions. Post-training can help it develop more familiarity with the data itself. Once we had that data foundation in place, the next step was making it easy to turn that information to professional-grade work. For financial professionals, that work often takes the form of an Excel model, a PowerPoint presentation, or a written analysis that needs to be reviewed and shared with other people. So we focused on helping the model produce those outputs in a way that fits the firm's existing workflows. We built a template system that gives users access to the firm's approved templates when generating spreadsheets and presentations. The goal is to reduce the work someone has to do to get an output ready for their team or clients. We also added things like interactive financial charts so users can explore stock prices and financial metrics directly within ChatGPT as they work through an analysis. And we built citation viewers that let people inspect the source passages and tables behind an answer. In finance, you need to be able to check where a number came from and understand the context around it. We wanted that review to be a natural part of the experience. These are the kind of product details that help turn a model's capabilities into work that someone can use. The part I think that is most relevant for people in the room is how we built it. Much of the functionality you just saw was built using the same ChatGPT plugin platform that's available to you as developers. For financial data, we used MCP tools and connectors to give the model access to the information it needs. We used citation metadata and MCP apps to let users inspect their sources, and MCP apps also power interactive financial charts. We used skills together with shared artifact tools to guide financial workflows and produce Excel models and PowerPoint presentations. And for financial onboarding, we leveraged the native plugin onboarding experience. What that means for builders is that you can focus on the expertise that makes your product valuable. If you have unique data, an existing tool, or a deep understanding of a particular workflow, you can use these building blocks to bring that into ChatGPT and create an experience around it. Financial services is just one example, but I do think this opportunity extends far beyond finance. I personally believe that we're going to see multiple $1 billion businesses built simply as ChatGPT plugins, and that opportunity will keep evolving as the models become more capable. Last but not least, I'd like to spend the rest of the talk on what comes next and what that means for the products we should be building today. I'd like to start by talking about model capabilities and expectations for the future. Models are improving so quickly that it can be difficult to get an intuitive sense of what comes next. One useful way to build that intuition is to look backwards. Something remarkable about the last couple of years is how predictable parts of that progress have been. Model improvements have come from three broad, sometimes overlapping drivers.
